utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody and welcome back. I hope everybody is well rested after the holidays and ready to work and work very hard. May the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Matthias Neuner for the Prosecution, assisted by our case manager Alma Imamovic-Ivanov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my learned friends of the OTP, to all those in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of Rasim Delic with assistants Lana Deljkic and Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it Mr. Neuner? Before you start, can we just swear in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for standing. Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may now be seated. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Could you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Ivan Negovetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: When and where were you born, Mr. Negovetic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo in 1939 on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can we please have exhibit -- can we please have document P 02652 shown to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you have your glasses?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I left them in that room back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: No problem. Could you tell us whose statement is this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. And did you sign each and every page of this statement, having read it before?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And after you have read and signed it, was this statement certified in November 2007 by a public notary in the United States?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that the content of this statement is accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to Rule 92 bis I would like to tender this statement of the witness dating 27th of November, with a PT number 6252 and the ERN number 06148894 till 06148903 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The statement is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 977, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to show you one document now, which you also discuss in the statement. The PT number is P 01306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it is P 01308 that my learned friend is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, correct. P 01308. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We see here it's a document from the 23rd of June, 1993, and if we could scroll -- if we could please go to the second page, I'm interested in the signatures. Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I signed it. My colleague Fadil Alihodzic did, and my superior, Mr. Stjepan Siber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we could go back to the first page again, please, and we see here it is sent to the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo and to the president of the Presidency of the RBih. If I may ask you who drafted that document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I drafted the first version of the document, which I then discussed with my colleague Fadil. We modified the initial version somewhat and this is the final version that the two of us agreed upon and presented to Mr. Siber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you mentioned your colleague Fadil. This would be Fadil Alihodzic who has also signed, just for clarification?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want you, please, to look at number 2 of this document and I see in the first sentence following number 2, it is stated in the village of Mehurici there are 247 civilians of Croatian ethnicity placed in a school gym. Have you yourself seen these people?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if I follow reading the document, the second sentence says: "They are under protection of the 306th military police but are exposed to mortal danger by the so-called death brigade, mostly consisting of Mujahedin, foreigners based in the immediate proximity." You explained to us you were the drafter. Could you explain to me what did you mean by the term "death brigade"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: This is the term I heard, or, rather the entire sentence was drafted based on my direct conversation with the battalion commander of the 306th Brigade, which we had had informally before the formal meeting. He relayed to me the facts contained in this sentence, namely, that under the protection of the 306th Brigade, and the police of the 306th Brigade that they protected them and that this Mujahedin brigade was called the death brigade. I heard that term from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you just explain to me where was this conversation with the battalion commander of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: In the primary school in a building in the village of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what did you mean by writing in this sentence that the Mujahedin are housed in the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I saw that they were accommodated on the first floor of the primary school building, that is to say, in the very same building where the civilians were accommodated, or rather, were situated in the gym where we visited them. On the ground floor, one unit of the 306th Brigade was billeted. I believe it was a battalion, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Can you explain what exactly you saw during your visit, what you saw about the persons which you consider to be part of this death brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: First, on the way to the village of Mehurici, several kilometres beyond that or away from that village a group of Mujahedins stopped us. We were in a vehicle of the UN and they pulled us over with -- they trained their anti-tank weapons at us. And Mr. Bagison, if I remember his name correctly, who was a member of the exchange commission asked the two of us, as members of the army, to get out of the car to see what it is that they wanted. I didn't know what was going on, because we were in a close-type vehicle. At any rate, he told us a to get out and negotiate with the people who pulled us over. We got out and noticed, observed a group of these individuals. I'm convinced that they were foreigners because they did not speak our language. I could only communicate with them in English. We asked them why they had stopped us and they said that we, as members of the army, the two of us were free to proceed but that the UN vehicle was not. We explained that in that case our mission would not be carried out and that we had to go as a whole that the other members of the commission were there. After these negotiations, we said that as a result of our mission not only those Croats would be released but also Muslims held as well elsewhere. I recall him asking me how many Muslims were involved and I gave him the figure of around 100 Muslims only to try and appease him. He then went behind some shrubbery, consulted someone there, went back and let us go. The people who stopped us were surely foreigners, both by their appearance and their manner of speech. As we entered the village of Mehurici, got out of our vehicle, and as we were entering the school building we noticed a group of the Mujahedin descending the stairs with anti-armor weaponry. They were shouting words in a language I did not understand and I concluded that they were foreigners too. They went somewhere - I don't know where - I entered the -- the building, I entered one of the classrooms and out of the windows there, observed what was going on. I noticed that they --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I just stop you here for a second. You said that these foreigners were coming down the stairs. What stairs of what building were they coming down?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the stairs of the primary school building in Mehurici. They were coming down the stairs from the first floor to the ground floor, and we passed each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, if you please go on with your observations.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Out of the window, we were able to see that they surrounded the vehicle with their anti-tank weapons trained at it. The situation was very tense. At that point, several soldiers, members of the army, came running out spontaneously. This was no order; they didn't even have any weapons on them. They stood between the Mujahedin and the UN vehicle and I believe that was what prevented the Mujahedin from opening fire. One by one they gave up and left until this just one person stayed who was the most pig-headed one but then he left in the end. And that was how this incident ended with no injuries on any side and that's my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, I thought this witness made a statement, a written statement and that you were just picking up on one or two things just to introduce the statement. It looks like we now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I fully agree but I was also tempted to interrupt the witness at certain stages but I failed. At this point in time it is maybe worth that I let him tell at least this episode. I will just ask him two, three more questions relating to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And please control your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I have just a question relating to the next, meaning the third sentence. You're referring to Mr. Salko Beba here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go a little bit up in the English, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Salko Beba allegedly said here that Mujahedin executed about 50 civilians. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, where did Mr. Beba explain that information to you, provide that information to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: At the command of the Operational Group Zapad, West, in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember any further details than what you have written down here already about this incident, the execution? Was Mr. Beba giving you any further details or was this about everything that you knew which you put down here in writing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: No, nothing else. The only thing which is contained in my statement is that he had told us this in confidence only to me and Mr. Fadil Alihodzic before the formal meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: He was doing his best not to have other members of the commission hear this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Then in the next sentence you mention a civilian who managed to survive this execution who would be among these 247 civilians in Mehurici. How did you learn this information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: This is part of the information we received from Mr. Salko Beba. After he told us about the execution, he said that one of them managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: After you had visited Mehurici on the 23rd of June, 1993, how long did you stay in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of August, just under two months therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. In the next paragraph here, it is mentioned that the complex Mujahedin -- that the issue with the Mujahedin would be a complex one. And -- or complicated, you write. And the president of the Presidency and the commander of the ARBiH should come to Zenica. Could you tell me what reaction, if any, did you get to this request?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I can only say that I don't know whether there was any reaction. I don't know anything about it. I can't say anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Fadil Alihodzic or Mr. Stjepan Siber, who as you explained had also signed this letter, told you something about a visit which you requested here by Mr. Izetbegovic or Mr. Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This means they didn't tell you anything, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: They didn't tell me anything, and I wasn't able to learn anything about it from any other sources of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, if Mr. Izetbegovic or Mr. Rasim Delic would have visited Zenica, would you, in your position as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that earlier my learned friend said that he was going to ask one or two questions pertaining to the letter. It appears to me that he is moving away from the letter and asking more general questions, some of which are touched upon in the statement already so I don't think it needs to be repeated by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The witness has in this letter requested such a visit and I'm just trying to follow up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but, you know, the testimony of the witness is contained in a paper, sir. That's what you wanted to put before this Court and I have just warned you about this earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Then the Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Negovetic. My name is Nicholas Robson and I represent General Rasim Delic today. As you will have gathered, your statement is admitted into evidence and the Trial Chamber will have read it. The purpose of me cross-examining you today is to clarify certain points contained within your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, may I interrupt you? I'm sorry to do this to you. Mr. Neuner, P 01308, do you want it admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 978, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So as I was explaining, the purpose is to clarify points contained within your statement. If at any time you don't understand my questions, please let me know and I'll try to rephrase the questions that I put to you. So, going to the background contained within your statement at paragraph 4 you explain how you became a member of the Supreme Command Staff of the ARBiH and that was in the second half of 1992. Could you tell us, what was your position within the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the administration of works, the two of us were actually charged. We were charged in the administration for biological, chemical -- for biological and chemical protection, Mr. Alija [as interpreted] and I.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you just please repeat the name, please. The interpreter didn't catch that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Mujo Alic and I were members of services for biological and chemical protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it right that your background was as a scientist and not as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: When I was recruited, yes. In fact, I completed the reserve officers school for atomic, biological and chemical warfare in the former Yugoslavia and it was probably on this basis that I was recruited into the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So but prior to you joining the Supreme Command Staff, you were a civilian. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your statement, you explain how you were ordered to go to the forward command post at Zenica. Before I explore what happened there, if I could just clarify a matter of terminology. At various points in your statement you refer to the Supreme Command and you say that you were appointed to the forward command post of the Supreme Command. Would you agree with me that in fact it was the Supreme Command Staff that you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was writing my statement in English and I must have made some errors in English. But that was the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just for clarification, the Supreme Command would in fact refer to the Presidency of the --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now if I could show you, please, Exhibit 245. Perhaps while we are waiting for that to appear, I could explain that this is an order for Supreme Command Staff to go to liberated territory and it is dated the 28th of April, 1993. Mr. Negovetic, can you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can just scroll to the bottom of the document in the B/C/S version and briefly go to page 2 in the English. We'll have to go to page 2 in the B/C/S as well; I apologise. Would you agree that here we can see that this order was issued by Sefer Halilovic, who was then the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. It was signed by someone on his behalf. I can't read or make out the name. But, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could revert back to page 1, please. Would you agree with me that in this order, Mr. Halilovic is ordering the various men who are to go to the forward command staff in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I can just make a suggestion, the witness has said that it wasn't signed by Mr. Halilovic. You were just putting to him that Mr. Halilovic has done certain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, would you agree that through this order what we can see, is that various members of -- or various officers are being sent to the forward command post at Zenica, and there at number 6, within paragraph number 2, we can see your name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me from paragraph number 1 in this document we can see that the purpose of the forward command post at Zenica was to monitor and to command armed combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Point number 1, I should say, rather than paragraph. Sorry, it is the very first paragraph that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading both versions, the English and ours but I don't see what you said. The first sentence says to activate the forward command post. And then responsible for providing working and living conditions and rations and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise if I have caused confusion. What I would like you to look at is if we look under the heading where it says order for SVK staff to go to liberated territory. Then there appears to be a line that sets out the purpose of the forward command post. And is it right or would you agree with me that the purpose of the forward command post was to monitor and command armed combat?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the first sentence says. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the area of responsibility of the forward command post, is it right that that related to Central Bosnia, in particular the zones of responsibility of the 2nd and 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: This is not explicitly stated here, but practically the 2nd and the 3rd Corps were within our range. We didn't have anything to do with other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just clear a point that causes me confusion, sir. Are you able to explain to us how these people were supposed to monitor and command armed combat in a liberated area? I would imagine that a liberated area, in a liberated area there would be no armed combat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this is question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course it is, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Zenica was -- you know that Sarajevo was under siege during the war and it was very difficult to organise the command in Sarajevo, I think. And one of the reasons to form this forward command post in Zenica was that, because Zenica was a relatively peaceful area - there were a couple of artillery attacks, perhaps, but in Zenica there was no armed conflict at that time that we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My point precisely. If there is it no armed combat there, how do you monitor armed combat there, in a liberated area or in an area that was never under attack? All I'm saying is that -- the words "under order" seem to contradict the way words below those words. I'm trying to get a reconciliation of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like the witness to assist. I'm not trying to trick you. If you are not able to explain, just say I can't explain; or if you have an explanation, you can give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The explanation that we got, when this forward command post was formed, was that it would be easier to command operations in the territory that was not under siege, like Sarajevo was. Because Sarajevo was under siege, that meant poor communications, complicated connections or communication with other units, so it was much easier to organise communication with other units in Zenica. I think that was the main reason. This is my opinion and this is also something that I had heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So as I understand it, Mr. Negovetic, you were based in Zenica, which was a relatively stable location subject to those artillery attacks that you mentioned, and from Zenica you yourself would go out into the field to visit various units and perhaps some of those units were in rather more dangerous locations. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement, you explained that you started your duties on the 2nd of May, and you explain how you visited various units at the corps and operations group level. And then you go on to explain that there were regular morning meetings at the forward command post. And what you say in paragraph 10 is, you had the impression that and I quote: "Information we received were significantly filtered. Also, we were not in a position to make any significant decision." And I would like to discuss that comment with you, if I may. Would you agree with me that the chain of command that was applicable to the Bosnian army dictated that information be sent from the corps level to the forward command post in Zenica and also to the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. We received numerous reports. I don't have proof of that, though. I can say that I do have the impression that were some reports that we didn't receive that we couldn't see. At least I didn't have the opportunity at our morning meetings to hear about them. This is difficult to explain but suddenly you would hear a piece of information from the other side or from the press even and it was something that you had never heard about at official meetings. Well, that was the impression that I formed. It could be erroneous. I'm not insisting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You're not insisting on that. Perhaps if I could show you a series of documents which relate to this very issue, and we can perhaps -- you can perhaps let us know whether you stick to that conclusion in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first document is D749. Your Honours, whilst we're waiting for this to appear on the screen, you will see that this is a regular combat report dated the 13th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, are you able to confirm that this report that we see in front of us was sent from the 3rd Corps command and we can see that it was sent to the Supreme Command of the RBiH. I think it may not be so clear for you from the front page, so what I will do is ask for us to take a look at the last page in this document in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can scroll down in the B/C/S, thanks. Sorry, scroll up in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I think just for the witness's assistance if we can just go to the page before this in the B/C/S version only and go to the bottom of this page, the copy is unfortunately cut off halfway through. But would you agree that that appears to be a stamp at the bottom and you may be able to make out the name, Hadzihasanovic, certainly the top part of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, the commander of the 3rd Corps, Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the final page in the B/C/S. So this document, dated 13th May which was not long after you arrived at the forward command post, would you agree that here, what we can see is on the very top line of this page, it says SVK, IKM and then the letters ZE, it looks like.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: SA? I think it is Sarajevo, SA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you look at the line below, the second line down from the top of the page, does that not say: SVK, SA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: In the second line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the second one would appear to be an indication that this document was sent to Sarajevo. If you look at the top line, would you agree that this shows that the report was sent to the forward command post at Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 979, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could turn to document D 750. Your Honours, I should say that I do have a number of these documents to show. I will try and keep them to the minimum but I will try and have the witness deal with them as swiftly as possible so as not to lose time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And here, Mr. Negovetic, would you agree that what we can see is a document in the same -- certainly with the appearance in the same form as before. In the English version it has a slightly different title, it says daily operations report with situation at 2200 hours. It's dated the 2nd of June, 1993. And if we look just next to the heading that I read out, would you agree that this -- that it shows that the report went to the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo and in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I don't see the bottom of the page, but I assume that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay, it's -- what I'm referring to you is on this page --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Oh yes. Yes, yes, I see it, yes. On the right side, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Sent to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this could be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 980, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could get you to turn to Exhibit D751. It is a regular combat report dated the 5th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If have you any difficulty in seeing these documents --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: [In English] I see it. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this is a regular combat report from the 3rd Corps. And again, when we look at -- next to the heading we can see that this document was sent to the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo and also in Zenica at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it could be please admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 981, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next document is D752. And while we're waiting, this document will be a regular combat report dated the 6th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And once again, Mr. Negovetic, from this -- I will just wait for the document to appear before the -- From this document, we can see that it was sent from the 3rd Corps to the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo and also the forward command post in Zenica. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Question? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this could please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 982, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could have a look at D753, please. Your Honour, while we're waiting, this is a regular combat report dated the 9th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, can you confirm that this is a report from the 3rd Corps to the Supreme Command Staff at Sarajevo and also to the forward command post in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now before we leave this document there is an item of interest that I would like to discuss with you and we can find it on the third page in the English version, and in the B/C/S version it is also page 3. Sorry, I apologise, it's page 2, the last paragraph in the B/C/S version. If we can scroll down the page in the English version. So here we have part of the report which deals with activities taking place around about the 9th of June, 1993. And what I'm interested in is the paragraph which is directly above point number 4. It's the last sentence in the B/C/S version, so, if you could please read that page and if we can turn over to the B/C/S version so you can see what it is that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph in English. I can see that the text correspond to each other. I'm sorry what was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I understand that you read both B/C/S and English, so I'm not sure which of the texts you're preferring to look at. What I'm interested in is in that text there is a sentence which says: The HVO is holding Velika Bukovica and Mala Bukovica with 150 detained civilians. Fighting is underway around the Velenici repeater. And my question to you is, this report from the 9th of June, that talks about detained civilians in Velika Bukovica, can you confirm that those were the civilians that you, yourself, saw in Skradno village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I saw a large group of people in the village of Skradno and I was told that some of them were the inhabitants of Skradno and some were refugees from the village of Bukovica. But I didn't ask, I didn't speak to the people, I didn't ask the people where they were from; we talked about other things. But it is possible that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Now, I think what I'll do is I'll come to your observations in the village of Skradno later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So at this stage, Your Honours, if this could please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 983, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could please look at D754. This is a regular combat report from the 3rd Corps dated the 14th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And once again, Mr. Negovetic, can you confirm that this report was sent from the 3rd Corps to the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo and the forward command post in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is obvious that that's what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If this could please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 984, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Next, Your Honours, D755. And this is the penultimate document from this type of document. Your Honours, while we're waiting for it to appear, this is a regular combat report from the 3rd Corps dated the 18th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, can you confirm that this report was sent to the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo and the forward command post in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it could please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 985, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then the final document of this type, it's D756, which is a regular combat report from the 3rd Corps, dated the 21st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Negovetic, can you again confirm that this is a report that went to the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo and in Zenica at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If this document could please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number 985, Your Honours -- I'm sorry, 986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We have just seen a range of documents over a period of time from early May until the 21st of June. Would you agree with me that these documents demonstrate that at least the 3rd Corps was reporting to both the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo and also its forward command post in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the shortest answer would be yes. But if you would like to hear my comments, then I could ... Do you want me just to answer with a yes or no or would you like me to explain a bit more? Brief explanation. We would receive about 20 of the reports like this every day, and throughout that whole period. When I was on duty at the staff, I would receive similar documents. I saw many of them, perhaps I can't recognise this particular one now, but a lot of them passed through my hands. There was a large number of them. What I'm not sure about is that if all of the documents were also sent to us. This is something that I have my doubts about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: All right. You satisfied my question, Mr. Negovetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is not satisfied. Sir, your statement and the part of that statement which resulted in this number of documents being tendered into evidence, states that: However, I have impression that information we received was significantly filtered. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That some of the documents were not shown to all members of the forward command post of the staff in Zenica. That is my impression, that, for example, I never saw a document relating to combat actions that resulted in the capture of Croatian civilians in the village of Mehurici, for example. That report I never did see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So what do you mean by this statement is that you did not receive -- you have the impression that you did not receive reports about everything that was taking place. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard about the event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you did not mean that the information you received was filtered. In other words, the information you received did not -- was not comprehensive enough by the time it reached you to be the same as it was when it was first compiled. There's a difference between -- you see, when you say the information was filtered is that you say you do receive the information but the information you are getting has details left out. That's not what you mean. What you mean is, you did not receive all the information that you could have received, or you should have received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be precise, documents that we received were the documents that we received. My impression, however, was that we did not receive all the documents that were sent to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that makes a difference to -- from what you have said in the statement. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just touching on that last answer, Mr. Negovetic. The reports that we just looked at over that period of time shows that information was going equally to Sarajevo and to Zenica. On what basis do you make the suggestion that you did not receive all the documents that were sent to Sarajevo? Do have you some specific information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not what the witness said. He hasn't said that he didn't receive all the information that was sent to Sarajevo. He says they did not receive all the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just quoting the last part of his response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Negovetic, do you have any basis upon which to claim that all the documents that were sent to Sarajevo did not go to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to provide any kind of specific proof, but I did hear about some events in talks with my colleagues or even reading the paper, but there was no sign of that in documents that we received. It doesn't mean that I saw each document with my own eyes. I saw the documents only when I was on duty at the operation centre, approximately once a week. Other documents were read to us in our morning briefings. I didn't actually look at them myself. Again, I say there were events that I never saw actually mentioned in documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that you are making an assumption that additional information was sent uniquely to Sarajevo, but in fact you don't know whether or not that was the case?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I assume something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask a question about this, if I may. We have been speaking about a number of events about which you received no reports in Zenica. What I would like you to specify is whether you heard about these events through someone who was a member of the Supreme Command and who stayed in Sarajevo, or else only from the media.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I didn't have contacts with members of the command in Sarajevo, only with those at the forward command post. Some of them had more information from sources other than the regular combat reports. We had the formal and informal meetings. Formal meetings involved the reading of the documents, we commented upon the documents and then possibly gave suggestions; and informal meetings where we discussed the situation in general and various events. In this way, I learned some information that I was unable to learn from regular reports. What made me suspicious the most, what in fact made me form this impression was that I never saw any of the reports relating to the events that I witnessed in the village of Mehurici. I never saw formally or heard formally of any document relating to the combat activities in the course of which 247 civilians were captured in and around the village of Mehurici. This is one example, based on which I concluded that not all the information reached me or at least not all the information was accessible to me. However, other individuals talked about this event. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another thing, but you do know whether concerning that particular event, i.e., the 247 civilians that you were aware of, you don't know whether or not this was reported to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, Mr. Negovetic, you say all strategic decisions were made in Sarajevo and we were barely informed about them. Now, earlier on in your testimony we ascertained that the work of the forward command post was concerned with monitoring and commanding within Central Bosnia. Would you agree with me that there would have been no need and it wouldn't have made sense for the forward command post to be concerned with decisions taken in Sarajevo that related to areas outside of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, concerning the area of Bosnia which the forward command post was responsible for dealing with, I'd like to show you some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could go into private session at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that whilst you were at the forward command post the bulk of your work related to carrying out these duties on checking that units were prepared for chemical and biological attacks?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: However, at some point you explain that you were appointed to a joint humanitarian commission for monitoring release of all prisoners and in paragraph 15 you say that the Supreme commander General Delic appointed you to the commission. Before I actually ask you about the commission itself, again, a matter of terminology, would you agree that the Supreme commander was in fact the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, that's down to my imprecision in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the role that General Delic held was in fact the commander of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in that same paragraph you discuss what you refer to as the Delic-Petkovic agreement, and what I propose is that after the break we'll come back and I'll ask you some more questions about that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, if we could perhaps take a break at this moment in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could take a look at the document establishing the joint humanitarian commission. Please, could document D757 be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Negovetic, this document is a little bit complicated because what we can see at the top of the page is that this is a document sent by the commander of the 3rd Corps, Enver Hadzihasanovic, dated the 12th of June, 1993, and below we can see that he is forwarding an order from another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps if we could go into private session at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In the English version, it's page 1 and the second paragraph I'm interested in, and in the B/C/S, it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Negovetic, I'm interested in the paragraph which begins: "We arrived Skradno from the direction of Zenica ..." It's --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if we look down through your diary, and first of all, perhaps I can ask you this. Do you recall when you prepared this diary extract? Would it have been the 23rd of June that you prepared it, or would it have been a day or so later?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Whenever I was able to, in the evening, I would write in my diary, and this day, which was actually full of events, quite shocking events, was something that I wrote about the next day. In the evening I was so tired that I couldn't write, so this was written the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we can say that this diary extract was written while events were still fresh in your mind.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In connection with the people at Skradno, you say: "We were surrounded by a large group of women, children and the elderly. Most of them originally came from the village of Velika Bukovica which has been completely torched." Velika Bukovica was a Bosnian Muslim village, is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, according to its population, yes. I mean in view of the refugees who had come from that village, yes. I had never seen that village before and after I never saw it again. So I don't know what happened, but judging by the refugees I assumed that it was a Muslim inhabited village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you actually see for yourself that it had been torched or was that something that somebody told you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: That's what the people that we talked to, people that we met there told us, the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the village had been completely torched during the HVO attack on it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I really cannot remember exactly how the combat proceeded. I can't remember exactly what was going on and even if I did see a document about that before or right now, I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, earlier on during the cross-examination we looked at a document that said that civilians from the village were being detained by the HVO. In Skradno village, in your diary, you describe how these civilians were living in a kind of ghetto and you say: "They can move freely within the village but they cannot leave the village, not even to visit a doctor or go shopping." Would you agree with me that the HVO was effectively keeping these people as prisoners against their free will?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct. I can also add that they kept this village as a kind of model village for foreigners, how well they were treating people who could cultivate the land and live in their houses. I think this is where they brought all these different international delegations to show them but actually these people were practically living like prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, for those people -- sorry, fortunately for those people who you saw in the village you were able to negotiate their exchange on the 24th of June, and that was with the civilians that were being held in Mehurici. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I informed -- I went to the Red Cross centre and informed them about these events. I think it was beyond our abilities to do anything about that, about any of these people, and as far as I'm concerned it was my biggest challenge in the war. I didn't in any way wish to be directly involved in the exchange of prisoners because I thought that that was a typical example of ethnic cleansing and I did not want to be accused one day of being organised or being a part of the organisation team for these exchanges. But I went to the Red Cross centre and asked them to do something and they did; they organised an exchange between the two for the people of Mehurici to be freed and to cross over into HVO-controlled territory and for the people from Skradno to move into the territory under the control of the armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So just so I'm clear about that, rather than being the joint commission that actually organised that exchange, it was the Red Cross, you say?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: In fact, the Red Cross put together Mr. Salko Beba, with -- and Pero Skopjak who were from the Bosnian and the HVO side respectively and the two of them actually organised the technical aspects of everything, and the Red Cross assisted in this exchange by providing their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we understand do you say -- or let me back-off a little bit. Am I right to say that the mandate of the commission to which you belonged was precisely to negotiate the release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. But it is one thing to free prisoners from prison and for them to choose where they would go and it's another thing to move people who live in one village to another village; this is something quite different. And at that time I was quite concerned that I would be doing something that would be against the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just talking about the negotiation according to the mandate of the commission, you were supposed to negotiate the release of these people together with your other commission members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat again, releasing people from prisons and camps is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just don't repeat. I'm asking you the question a second time because your answer is not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm repeating myself so that you can answer my question directly. Am I right, sir, that the mandate, the instructions to your commission was to negotiate the release of prisoners of war on both sides? You can answer me by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. You then delegated that job to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you abdicated your duties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, as I said, it was a very big moral dilemma for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, you can answer me yes or no. You abdicated your duties, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: According to your statement, after Skradno village you then visited or travelled towards Mehurici and in the statement you how for the first and only time you encountered foreign Mujahedin. Just so I'm clear, there is the 23rd of June, 1993, that you travelled to Mehurici village and encountered the Mujahedin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, on that day, you travelled in an UNPROFOR vehicle, and you described how the Mujahedin stopped the vehicle by pointing its weapons at you. It's right to say that those foreign Mujahedin fighters that you saw were well armed.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: They had light infantry and anti-tank weapons. The light infantry weapons that they had were automatic AK 47 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: From what you told us today it was about seven kilometres outside of Mehurici that they stopped the vehicle. And in your diary, you mention that the Mujahedin stopped you somewhere in the region of Guca Gora. Is it correct that it was in the region of Guca Gora that you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where they stopped us because I was in the vehicle and I couldn't really follow where we were going. Only when I came out of the vehicle to negotiate with them, I was in an area that I was not familiar with, I had never visited it before. I know that that whole broader area is called Guca Gora, not just one place and that is what I put down in the diary. As for exactly where it happened, I assume, I don't know, maybe it was a couple of kilometres later. We drove for another ten or 20 minutes and reached Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, this was the first and only time that you actually saw foreign Mujahedin. But had you ever heard there were different Mujahedin groups around that area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: To this day, I don't know who exactly was there. The only thing that I do know is that the -- the corps were foreigners but also our people were also members of the El Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You were able to continue with your journey, and you've explained how -- when you got to Mehurici there was a further incident. And at paragraph 33 of your statement you describe how when you got out of the vehicle the Mujahedin surrounded the vehicle with offensive weapons ready to use. Salko Beba was with you at that moment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: As I was observing the events, the battalion commander of the 306th Brigade was with me. Salko Beba was not close to me. He was somewhere near me. I didn't really see him that much, other than at our regular meeting that took place after that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just considering Salko Beba for a moment, was he somebody that you knew? Was he somebody that you had met prior to the 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: No, the first time I met him was in Travnik that day, and also when we went to visit the OG-7. I never heard of him before that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You have referred to him as being a member of OG Zapad, OG West. Would you agree with me that in fact Salko Beba worked for OG Bosanski Krajina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: It is possible, but it was strange that he was there in Operations Group West, and I didn't think that he belonged there, but somebody said that he was in intelligence -- actually, no, that he was in charge of security in that area. I don't know exactly which unit he belonged to by establishment. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And earlier in your evidence when you were asked questions by the Prosecutor, you said that you met Salko Beba in OG Zapad in Travnik. Would you agree with me that OG Zapad is in fact based in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: It's possible. This is something that I put in my diary. What I actually said in my statement is based on things from my diary, so if I made a mistake, it means that I made a mistake in the diary and I don't know why. I mean, that is something that is a bit odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just to clarify, it was the command of OG Zapad that I was putting to you was in Bugojno. Now, what you've said in your statement about this moment in time and it's at paragraph 28, is that: "It looked to me that the foreign fighters acted on their own." So amongst you present in Mehurici were members of the 306th Brigade, somebody from the local operations group, and yourself and Fadil Alihodzic, who were members of the Supreme Command Staff. Would you agree with me that none of you could command the Mujahedin that you met with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: We definitely did not in any way. The two of us members of the Supreme Command Staff, they did not respect. The first time they intercepted us they behaved in a hostile manner even though we were wearing Bosnian army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt before I lose this page. At line 16, page 51, Mr. Robson you said: "And earlier in your evidence when you were asked questions by the Prosecutor you said that you met Salko Beba in OG Zapad in Travnik. Would you agree with me that OG Zapad is in fact based in Bugojno?" And then the witness gave an answer and then you said: "And just to clarify, it was the command of OG Zapad that is --" I'm sorry, the English here is typed incorrectly. It was the command of OG Zapad that I was putting to you was in Bugojno. What were you saying there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was making a clarification that it was the command of OG Zapad that we were suggesting was based in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not Salko Beba.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's correct. The command of OG Zapad and not Salko Beba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is the position of the -- of the Defence about Salko Beba? Was he part of OG Zapad or was he part of something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The Defence's position is that he was a member of OG Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, it's just a matter -- the purpose of asking those questions is just to really establish what the witness knew of Salko Beba and whether he had an erroneous recollection of that person's details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, and for the Court to be satisfied that we have established that his recollection is erroneous it must understand what your position is and what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, in paragraph 37 of your statement you say that you went into the room where the civilians were being kept. You also say that the prisoners were being supervised by the Bosnian army. Would you agree with me that it was municipal civilian protection staff that was responsible for looking after the civilians at the school?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me anything to that effect. What I was told was that the military police of the 306th Brigade was taking care of that. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I didn't double-check that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could please bring Defence document up on the screen. It is it D760.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we are moving to the next document the Prosecution would just like to know whether the document just shown to the witness, D748, is tendered by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will be, yes, please, if it could be admitted into evidence. The reason I didn't ask is that I will be returning back to this document. But if it could be admitted at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can come back to it as an exhibit already. The document D748 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 990, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the correct B/C/S version of the document that I'm after, and here is the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So this is the cover page, Mr. Negovetic. Just to explain, this is a series of documents. I don't wish to take up the Court's time going through every page. But can you see that the cover page states: Request to initiate proceedings, against two named persons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And at the top we can see that this bears a stamp which speaks of the Travnik municipality civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer to -- I believe it's page number 4 in the English version, and in the B/C/S -- this is the correct page. In the B/C/S it should be page 4 as well. Could you confirm that what we see here is a letter dated the 23rd of June, 1993, from the commander of the Travnik municipality, municipal civilian protection staff and it's addressed to the Travnik municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the first part of this letter, under the heading states: "In the course of transport of food for refugees in Mehurici and Gluha Bukovica and persons in the primary school, the following supplies disappeared." Would agree with me that what this document shows is that the municipal civilian protection staff had a responsibility for caring for those persons who were in the primary school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have listened to the course of the introduction of the document and so on, what is unclear to us is what the relationship between the witness and this particular document should be. It is a document from the municipal staff and if I understood it correctly, it is sent to another civilian organ so according to us, it has not passed the witness's desk. And we just don't understand at this point in time, when such questions are asked, what the relationship between the witness and this document should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness attended at Mehurici. He is purporting to tell the Court things that he saw, things that he learned and on a number of occasions this witness has changed his version. He has accepted that in hindsight things were rather different from how he has stated them in his statement. And, Your Honour, I would suggest that this is a similar situation, that we have the opportunity to put the contents of this document to the witness to see if he is able to comment, and -- and I believe it is a matter that we can look at it in the -- in due course at the right moment. But I don't believe it is correct for the Prosecution to stand up and object to us asking questions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you raise your neck, Mr. Neuner. Are you attempting to stand up?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not saying you should. Do you want to stand up?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Our position would be, Your Honours, this is a document which may deal with logistics. The witness have -- has told the Chamber what he has learned on the occasion of his visit to Mehurici; he was told that the military police was performing a certain job. And we don't understand that the witness who was not travelling there in relation to logistical issue should comment upon an issue which deals with the supply of items such as litres of oil and other things, how he should be in a position to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Robson, if I may come in here, your introduction of this document, as I understood your train of thought was to try to disprove that the military police were in charge but that the civilian police were in charge or that the municipal police were in charge. I'm not quite sure how this document does disprove that. It does -- it does prove one thing, that the municipal police were also involved in the exercise. I'm not sure whether it takes us much further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have touched on the correct point. It's been suggested that only the Bosnian army was involved in the care and what we're trying to show is -- through these documents is that it was uniquely the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's be quite clear what was said. Was it said that only the army was involved or was it said that the military police were involved, from the witness. I don't remember him using the word "only".

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, according to your statement and I don't have the paragraph number in front of me, I believe you said it was the military police of the ARBiH that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what he was told when he was there. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was told but based on what I was able to see there, I didn't see anybody else in the school building other than members of the Bosnian army who were present on the ground floor and on the first floor. So I didn't see anybody else but them, and I was told that it was the military police of the 306th Brigade that was taking care of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you exclude the possibility that it was the civilian police that was charged with looking after these civilians in the school, and that the Bosnian army was giving assistance to them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you're asking the witness to speculate now, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would seek still to -- attempt to touch upon this document to see whether it is capable of being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure -- let's just understand first what the purpose of Mr. Neuner's objection was because we have to rule on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The purpose of my objection was to find out the link between the witness and the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you found it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It can be marked for identification, Your Honours. And the Defence is invited to maybe call another witness during the course of their case which can shed further light on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mean another witness will come and establish the link between this document and this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Between this document and the fact who was responsible for running the refugee --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do they need this document to prove that fact? That witness can just come and tell us who was running.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I myself don't understand why this particular document is being shown to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is your objection, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The link between the witness and the document, since this document has not passed the witness as desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are you objecting to the tendering of this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's better. You said you're objecting to the link. Be clear. Mr. Robson, there is an objection to the tendering of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will withdraw the document and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But if we could have it please marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I don't withdraw the document. What I would do is I would please ask that it be marked for identification and we'll see if we can deal with it during the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI 991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, I would like to return to what you have told us about what you saw while were at the school. In your statement, you have explained to us that you met with the local army battalion commander who was based in that village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how he introduced himself to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. You have also told us about an incident that occurred outside the school involving the Mujahedin. What I'd like to do is come back to your diary dealing with the events on the 23rd of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could please bring that document back up. It is Exhibit 999, and it's page 2 that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say Exhibit 999? We haven't reached that number yet, sir, of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise, it's 990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So this is your diary which you've told us was written while events were still fresh in your memory. If you can look at the -- if we could look at the -- it's the page after in the English, please. And it's the third paragraph that I'm interested in, which begins: "We arrived Mehurici." In the B/C/S version it is the next page as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of clarity about exhibits, was Exhibit 990 not an extract from this diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you're looking at some other part of the diary which is not part of Exhibit 990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Exhibit 990 is a document which comprises three pages in English and it deals solely with the events on the 23rd of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it includes this page that you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So what this says is: "We arrived in Mehurici after almost an hour, an hour of uncomfortable drive. As soon as we left the vehicles and entered the school accommodating Croat refugees, a commotion began.
