A group of Mujahedin who suddenly appeared out of nowhere surrounded the UNPROFOR armed personnel carriers and pointed the anti-armour weapons." Now, in your testimony a little earlier today what you said was when you entered the school the first thing you saw was Mujahedin coming down the stairs. That contradicts the version that we see here in your diary. Can you explain for us why we have the two different versions of events?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I don't see the difference. If all at once you see someone coming down the stairs in a building you never entered before, that can be described as all of sudden, out of nowhere, but to be specific, yes, I saw them coming down the stairs. This was something that happened to me suddenly. It was surprising and shocking and I may have described it in a way that was perhaps literally, but the truth is that I saw them with my own eyes coming down the stairs. I didn't expect to see them there to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But you don't mention anything in the diary about them coming down the stairs. Let me ask you this: Do you remember where the vehicles were parked when you got out and made your way towards the school? Were they parked in the middle of the street?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: They were parked in the school yard, several dozen metres away from the gate leading to the school yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Because the way that I certainly read your statement is that this group of Mujahedin who suddenly appeared out of nowhere and surrounded the UNPROFOR armoured vehicles, it sounds as though that they were outside of the school when they suddenly appeared.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: No. They had come out of the school. I still have this image vivid in my mind, and I am not mistaken there. I saw them coming down the stairs, carrying weapons. I didn't know what their intention was. They went past me outside, whereas I went upstairs to one of the classrooms where I observed what was going on out of one of the windows there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me move to something else that you talk about in your diary. You have told us today that these Mujahedin were stationed in the school on the first floor. But if we can look at the next paragraph down in your diary, it's on this page. And it's the paragraph that begins: "After brief persuasion, the Mujahedin went away."

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what this says here, and you've recorded it in your diary: "Later on the army battalion commander told me just between him and me, that those Mujahedin were great evil for the area. They are accommodated there in the surrounding of Mehuric and some 60 of them, together with local Muslim extremists form a death brigade." So here you have recorded what you were told by the battalion commander, that those Mujahedin were not accommodated in the school, but they were in the surrounding area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: That's what he told me. And I described what I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: See, in this diary extract and we can look at it in detail, if necessary, at no place do you mention that the Mujahedin were accommodated in the school. Could it be that your recollection perhaps is not so clear and what you recorded in your diary while events were still fresh in your mind is the accurate version; in other words, that the Mujahedin were accommodated in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not quite sure I understand this line of questioning. The fact that people are accommodated in surrounding area doesn't preclude their presence in a school at a particular time. And the witness has not -- has not testified that they were accommodated in the school. He says he saw them come down the stairs in the school. He doesn't -- at least what he has been saying to us today. He saw them come down. Where they are accommodated, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it was so simple, I wouldn't be elaborating the point. Within paragraph 35 of the statement it states: "I noticed that that both the Bosnian army and Mujahedin were stationed in the same school," so that is the point that I'm dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I won't take issue with the word "stationed." Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Negovetic, I was trying to ask you about the discrepancy between what was recorded in your diary, which was made while events were still fresh in your mind and the statement that you prepared not so long ago.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. I'm not disputing that you saw Mujahedin there at the school. Could it be that you are wrong when you concluded that the Mujahedin were stationed at the school and could it be the case that in fact as the local army battalion commander explained to you, those Mujahedin were accommodated in the surroundings -- or in the surrounding of Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: First, I remember them absolutely very well, that they came down the stairs. This image remained stuck in my mind. You know how sometimes certain shocking things that you witness remain in your -- remains in your mind, with the weapons. And this conclusion comes as a result of that, because if a unit comes rushing out of a place, then the natural conclusion is that they are billeted there. I saw some writings in Arabic on the wall running along the stairs. Everything was logically leading me to conclude that they were indeed stationed there and that's why I wrote that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just so I understand that clearly, the basis of your -- for you concluding that they were stationed at the school was because you saw a number of Mujahedin coming down the stairs.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Weapons. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Negovetic, the transcript captured the word weapons there. I'm not whether you misunderstood my question or not. Perhaps I better repeat it. Is it right that for the basis for you concluding that the Mujahedin were stationed at the school was because you saw a number of Mujahedin coming down the stairs?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I repeat. I saw them come out with weapons and if you see somebody coming out of a place with weapons then that's the basis for a conclusion that they are stationed there. Had they stormed out without weapons, well, then -- but the important thing is to say that they came out with weapons, and on the basis of that one concludes that they are stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 36 of your statement you say that a commander of the Bosnian military unit in Mehurici told you that the Mujahedin harassed and abused Muslim civilians and he was ready to attack if the Supreme Command commanded them to. I'd like to ask you about this, again by referring to your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's at page 3 of the diary that I'm interested in, in the English version. I apologise. If we can remain on this page for just a moment, we will just deal with the last sentence on this page. I don't know if we have the corresponding part in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if we look at this last paragraph, here you relate the conversation that you had with the local commander and he talks about the Mujahedin and he says: "They are attempting to introduce the Shariah law in the territory. They are ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could look on to the next page in English. So they are attempting to introduce the Shariah law in the territory they are staying in, however, for whatever reasons the 3rd Corps command does not want to have a showdown with that death brigade. So according to the diary, Mr. Negovetic, the commander referred to the 3rd Corps and not the Supreme Command. And I have looked through this diary and for that entire day there's no mention of the Supreme Command or Supreme Command Staff. Would you agree with me that it is more likely that the local commander used the words that you recorded in the diary at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I described here what I had heard from him. He was very upset at that incident and very angry. Obviously he was very uncomfortable with the entire situation and that was probably the reason why he told me all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And from what the commander told you, it's clear that he did not consider the Mujahedin to be allies of the Bosnian army or of any use to the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have too many more questions, but perhaps if we could take the break now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We shall indeed take the break now and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, in your statement, when you are describing what happened while you were in Mehurici village, you say: "The story we heard there from the local commander was that Mujahedins attacked a Croat village nearby, killed some of the inhabitants and arrested survivors." Now, according to the proofing note that you made with the Prosecution when you saw the Prosecutor yesterday, the 14th of January, you changed this part of your statement. Is that correct? Is it the case that you realised that it wasn't the local commander that gave you this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the briefest possible way put, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And so, is it the case that, having arrived in The Hague when you thought again over the facts of what had happened, you came to the conclusion that it was Salko Beba who told you that piece of information contained in paragraph 38?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: The following is true. I understood that that item in the statement did not actually correspond to the facts right from the beginning, so I was thinking, if I should sign the statement or not, but, it seemed to me that that part could be interpreted in various ways. It could be taken to mean -- I didn't compose that statement; I responded to questions that were sent to me by the investigator and I -- and memos that he sent me. He actually drafted the entire statement on the basis of my answers, and it seems to me that the way it was drafted does not correspond exactly to what I intended to say, but I didn't want to make anything of it. I was thinking should I sign it or should I not sign it, but I still I signed it fully aware that that paragraph, 38, in fact is just repeating what I said before, that I had heard this thing from Salko Beba. Local commander to me meant Mr. Salko Beba, although I'm not even sure to this day exactly what his function was. So that is the brief story of this paragraph. And when I came here I had a conversation with the Prosecutor and I insisted that this be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you have clarified paragraph 38, that the information contained in there is not correct. But if I can ask you this: Earlier on in your testimony today I showed you an order establishing the joint commission, and you accepted that part of your duties, as a member of that commission, included identifying criminals in cooperation with the military Prosecutor's office and the military court. Now, no matter who the source of this information was, you've said that you heard that Mujahedin attacked the village, killed some inhabitants and arrested some survivors. Did you take steps to contact a military Prosecutor's office to inform them of what you had learnt?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: (redacted). We felt that the best thing would be to inform -- well, the scale of this event seemed so large that it seemed to us that it was best if we informed the Supreme Command or the Supreme Command Staff about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you've told us you informed General Siber. You've accepted that you had an obligation to cooperate with the local military Prosecutor's office. Did it ever cross your mind to get in contact with the Military Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I must admit that it did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 39 of your statement you talk about information that you gather --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you answer that, Mr. Negovetic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: First, we informed him verbally, as soon as we returned from Mehurici, Mr. Fadil Alihodzic and myself informed him and then we talked about it, and he believed, I mean, his suggestion was that I write a draft -- I'm sorry, I'm forgetting the words of our language. A draft, and then the next day that we discuss it and then that this is sent to the Supreme Command, that this would be the best reaction to this report, I mean, to what we saw and experienced there. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that what I said indicates

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I think the turn of questions took a bit of an unexpected turn. So I apologise and we should have, perhaps, jumped into private session a little sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there anything that you suggest should be redacted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, we heard from the journalist that asked the question that that press conference took place 18 months after the start of the war, and we heard General Delic's response to the question and how he made it clear that he wanted a multi-ethnic Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you agree with me that up until the end of the war, despite all the difficulties, there were Serbs and Croats, or men of Serb and Croat ethnicity that remained within the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: That's true, but not for the Supreme Staff. I believe I was the last one to be there. When I returned from Zenica, I was transferred to an isolated post which had nothing to do with the work of the Supreme Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We saw at the table that General Divjak was present. He remained a deputy commander of the Supreme Command Staff until the end of the war, did he not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this exactly at this time. I believe he was retired before, but I will not give you a yes or no answer because I don't know; however, I know that (redacted) was appointed a military attache in Switzerland, that Mr. Divjak was retired or something else, but except for the two of them, I was the last one to have been part of the active operative --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but I see there is a technical problem. The answer could not be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, can we just wait for the stenographer to sort her problems out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to repeat the answer that you were saying just before we stopped or do you want the question put to you or do you want to read it there and try to answer it again, sir? The question put to you was: "We saw at the table that General Divjak was present. He remained a deputy commander of the Supreme Command Staff until the end of the war, did he not?" That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is, I can't remember if he remained there until the end of the war. That's what I meant. I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the record, if I might interrupt, Mr. Robson, what ethnic group do you belong to, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And General Divjak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Negovetic, you mention that -- you mentioned something along the lines of the -- within the Supreme Command Staff you did not see members of other ethnicity remaining within that organisation. And I apologise if I've misphrased your response. Would you agree with me, though, that within the Supreme Command Staff, until the end of the war, Ivan Brigic served as the chief of the administration for morale and he - I'm told the pronunciation is Brigic - and he is a man of Croatian ethnicity, Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question. I can only speak of the operational section, about the administration of services and I'm sure that in that segment there were none. When I returned from Zenica, I don't recall meeting any one of them there. I do recall Mr. Brigic. He was a professor and he probably performed that function, but to me he appeared more of a civilian than a soldier. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And finally, how about Zeljko Grubesic? He was a man who served in the cabinet of General Delic and he also was a man of Croat ethnicity. Are you aware of him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGOVETIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Robson, before you leave the witness, I'm unsure about the theme and the importance of this last line of questioning. And I -- because I'm sitting back with the impression that what the witness is really saying is that despite the good intentions expressed by General Delic and others to have a multi-ethnic leadership of the army, despite all those good intentions, nevertheless, the leadership ended up being ethnically Muslim or overwhelmingly Muslim, and I want to just have the witness clarify --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find a brief answer, but it's hard. First of all, in the middle of the war, the division of Bosnia and the division of the different ethnic groups became deeper and deeper. And I must say that at the start of the war some people from the armija deserted into the HVO; the erosion of the armija probably started with that process. That is one part of the answer. The other one is that within the armija itself and within the staff of the Supreme Command, very extremist individuals emerges with their convictions. I believe that General Bijajac [phoen] stated in my presence, We have to break free or we have to cleanse the Armija of the Serb and Croat elements. I heard him utter these words in my presence whilst I was still in the administration, not of services but in the administration of schools. He was quite extremist. What sort of influence he wielded in the Armija, I don't know; but I believe that these people contributed greatly to the army being mono-ethnic. It wasn't of course also due to them. The situation was very complex it all ended up with a full division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How unfortunate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Neuner? Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, please could -- two things. Please could the video be admitted into evidence, first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: VD-16 is admitted into evidence. Is it under seal or not? No, it's not under seal. Could it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And also I note that the record as I look at my colleague's screen it's page 3, line 5, on this computer screen, doesn't accurately reflect the witness's answer. I just hope that it can be rectified. It seems ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where, sir, line five?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Page 3, line 5, on the screen in front of my colleague. It should -- it says something along the lines some people from the armija diverted into the HOCK, the diversion probably started and what the witness clearly stated was that some people deserted from the army into the HVO. So, certainly, we hope that can be rectified in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that it is rectified. Thank you very much. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have just issue to address, Your Honours, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Negovetic, it was a couple of times mentioned during the cross-examination by my learned colleague, the question: Who in the Supreme Command received information about your visit of the joint humanitarian commission to Travnik and Mehurici and the information about possible crimes connected on occasion of this visit to Travnik and Mehurici. And for the record, this was in relation to Exhibit 170, also in relation to page 69 of today's transcript and page 74 of today's transcript. And before I go on, could we maybe move into private session because I'm going to address some issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess due to the lateness of the hour we're going to have to stop at this stage. Court adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of January, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
